# Psalm 33: verse-by-verse research notes

**Notes on sources:** I couldn't get NET Bible notes, Wesley's own notes, oca.org, catholic.com, or any Pentecostal, Lutheran or prosperity/word-of-faith teaching on this psalm, so those are left out. The tradition labels (for example "Methodist" for Clarke, "Anglican" for the Pulpit Commentary) are my own identifications. The pages themselves don't state them.

---

**Overview**
- An older commentary on Bible Hub divides the psalm into three reasons to praise God: his goodness, Psalm 33:1-5; of his power, Psalm 33:6-11; and of his providence, Psalm 33:12-15, followed by a promise of mercy for those who fear him (vv. 16–22). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-1.htm
- Utley (bible.org) notes the psalm has no title. He argues the "new song" implies some major historical event. Because of Ps. 33:16-17, probably it refers to a military victory. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-33

**v. 1**
- Guzik: the "righteous" are mainly God's people who live rightly. Under the New Covenant we may extend this to those declared righteous through faith in Jesus (Romans 3:21-26). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-33/
- Spurgeon: praise sounds wrong coming from the unforgiven. Crooked hearts make crooked music, but the upright are the Lord's delight. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-1.htm
- Barnes: if a person is upright, that is itself a reason to praise, because their character comes from God's grace. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/33.htm
- Augustine (Catholic/patristic): rejoice in the Lord, not in yourselves, "for that is not safe." https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.XXXIII.html

**v. 2: a real Protestant disagreement about musical instruments in worship**
- Guzik (Calvary Chapel, close to the charismatic tradition): the psalmist plainly calls for instruments, and it is "strange" that some have limited them to the Old Covenant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-33/
- Geneva Study Bible (Reformed): playing instruments was a part of the ceremonial service of the temple, which does not belong to us any more than the sacrifices, censors and light. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-2.htm
- Spurgeon (Baptist) takes a middle position. He sees instruments as Israel's training aids, saying in these days, when Jesus gives us spiritual manhood, we can make melody without strings and pipes. But he will not call them unlawful, and leaves those who use them to "gospel liberty." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-1.htm
- Catholic: Aquinas records an objection that the Church avoided harps and psalteries for fear of seeming to imitate the Jews. Against that, he defends the use of song: the use of music in the divine praises is a salutary institution, that the souls of the faint-hearted may be the more incited to devotion. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/3091.htm
- Church Fathers read the ten strings symbolically. Augustine takes them as the Ten Commandments, kept in love of God and neighbour (ccel link above). Clement of Alexandria asks whether the ten-stringed psaltery indicate the Word Jesus, who is manifested by the element of the decad? https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/02092.htm
- On the instruments themselves: Pulpit and Barnes say the Hebrew probably means one instrument, a ten-stringed lute or psaltery, rather than two. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-2.htm

**v. 3**
- Boice, quoted by Guzik: every "new song" should come from a fresh awareness of grace. Kidner, also quoted by Guzik, notes the verse asks for freshness, skill and fervour together. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-33/
- Spurgeon: It is wretched to hear God praised in a slovenly manner. He deserves the best that we have. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-1.htm
- Benson gives two readings of "new song": a song newly written for a new occasion, or songs renewed and repeated day by day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-2.htm
- Augustine: the new song is a song "of the grace of faith." (ccel link above)

**v. 4**
- Matthew Henry: God's word is right, and therefore all our deviations from it are wrong. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_033.cfm
- Barnes: "in truth" is better translated "in faithfulness." That is, All that he does is executed faithfully. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-33.html
- Clarke (Methodist): All the words, laws, promises, and threatenings of God are perfectly true and just. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-33.html
- Augustine's Latin text reads "done in faith." He uses it to argue that no one reaches faith through the merit of works. (ccel link above)

**v. 5**
- Guzik: God is "not amoral." VanGemeren, quoted by Guzik, says God shows all creation the same covenant loyalty (*hesed*) he shows Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-33/
- Henry: God never did nor can do wrong to any of his creatures, but is always ready to give redress to those that are wronged. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_033.cfm
- Augustine reads "mercy and judgment": mercy shown first, judgment later, and sins forgiven throughout the world. (ccel link above)

**v. 6: Protestant commentators divide over whether this verse points to the Trinity**
- Trinitarian reading. Gill (Baptist) takes "word" as Christ and "breath" as the Holy Spirit. He adds that we are not to suppose that one Person took one part, and another Person another part of the creation. Spurgeon agrees: the three persons of the Godhead unite in creating all things. Henry says the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-6.htm
- Calvin (Reformed) accepts that the world was made by the eternal Word, the Son. But he points to Isaiah 11:4 and says "breath of his mouth" just means speech, so In proving the Divinity of the Holy Spirit, therefore, I durst not press this text against Sabellius. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/33-6.html
- Poole and Benson (Methodist) give both readings without choosing. Ellicott: the breath is plainly only a synonym for word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-6.htm ; https://biblehub.com/psalms/33-6.htm
- The Cambridge Bible, closer to modern scholarship: The germ of the doctrine of the Word in John 1:1; John 1:3 may be found here, though of course the Psalmist had no idea of a personal Word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-6.htm
- R. A. Torrey and Abraham Kuyper both use this verse when writing about the Holy Spirit's work in creation. https://biblehub.com/context/psalms/33-6.htm
- Augustine reads it spiritually: the "heavens" are the righteous, strengthened by the Word, and their faith comes by the Holy Spirit. (ccel link above)

**v. 7**
- Barnes: "gathering" is a participle, so the verse describes a continuous act; an act not merely of the original creation, but constantly occurring. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-33.html
- Pulpit: the verse alludes to creation, with a glance at the Red Sea and Jordan crossings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-33.html
- Augustine follows his Latin text ("as into a bottle") and reads it as God gathering the peoples to confess their sin. (ccel link above)

**v. 8**
- Pulpit: The righteous alone have a right to "praise" God (see Psalms 33:1), but "all the earth"—i.e. all mankind—may be called upon to "fear" him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-33.html
- Utley: YHWH, not nature, is to be feared. The enemy of biblical faith today in western societies is "naturalism," https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-33

**v. 9**
- Barnes: the translators' added word "done" weakens the line. The Hebrew is simply "He spake, and it was." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-33.html
- Guzik links the verse to the centurion's faith in Luke 7. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-33/

**v. 10**
- Barnes: any human purpose opposed to God's plans will be rendered futile or vain. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-33.html
- Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik: Satan's cunning is outwitted by infinite wisdom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-33/

**v. 11**
- Spurgeon (Calvinist Baptist) reads the verse as predestination: God has a predestination according to the counsel of his will, and none of the devices of his foes can thwart his decree for a moment. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps033.cfm
- Henry: God's counsel can be opposed, but it can never be blocked. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_033.cfm

**v. 12: who is "the nation"?**
- Pulpit (Anglican) takes it strictly as Israel: One "nation" or "people" only is spoken of, viz. the Hebrews. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-12.htm
- Barnes: the verse refers first to Israel, but it is true of every people who worship the true God. Gill: the "chosen generation" drawn from both Jews and Gentiles. Another commentary on the same page stresses election: Election is at the bottom of it all. The divine choice rules the day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-12.htm
- Henry: Israel, and also all who own God, for they also, whatever nation they are of, are of the spiritual seed of Abraham. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_033.cfm
- Augustine: the one blessed nation belongs to the heavenly city, chosen by God's gift and not by its own doing. (ccel link above)

**vv. 13–14**
- Henry: atheists suppose God, living in heaven, takes no notice of earth, but from there he sees everyone. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_033.cfm
- Spurgeon: the thought is repeated because people easily forget it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps033.cfm
- Augustine reads God's "prepared habitation" as the human nature Christ took on. (ccel link above)

**v. 15: what does "He shapes the hearts" mean?**
- Barnes (Presbyterian): it does not mean God makes the heart good or bad. The point is that the Maker knows what is inside. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/33-15.htm
- Gill: from this verse he argues that souls are created, not generated. He also says God re-forms the hearts of his own people. (Same page)
- Pulpit: God's gracious influences shape hearts, but Some hearts are too stubborn to yield themselves up to his fashioning. (Same page)
- Augustine: God gives each heart its own spiritual gifts, as in 1 Corinthians 12. (ccel link above)

**v. 16**
- Henry: David, a king and warrior, still saw God as his only protector. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_033.cfm
- Augustine applies the verse to the inner life: no one wins against lust or the devil by trusting his own strength. (ccel link above)

**v. 17**
- Barnes: "vain thing" is literally a "lie," meaning the horse cannot be trusted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-33.html
- Pulpit draws a dating point: the familiar use of horses in war suggests the writer must have lived later than the time of David. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-33.html

**vv. 18–19**
- Pulpit: God's eye is on everyone in a sense, but it rests especially upon the righteous. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-33.html
- Henry limits the promise in a way that is relevant to prosperity teaching (though I found no prosperity teacher's comment on this psalm). God does not say that he will give them abundance (they have no reason either to desire it or to expect it), but he will keep them alive. He adds that even If he do not deliver the body from temporal death, yet he will deliver the soul from spiritual and eternal death. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_033.cfm
- Constable is similarly careful: God normally chooses to bless those who fear Him and rely on His promised love. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-33.html
- Augustine reads the famine as spiritual, and the food as "the nourishment of the Word." (ccel link above)

**v. 20**
- Pulpit: we trust no one but God, not armies, horses or our own strength. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-33.html
- Ellicott: Hebrew has many words for hope and waiting, which fits a nation whose golden age lay in the future. https://biblehub.com/psalms/33-20.htm
- Spurgeon: notice the three "ours" in vv. 20–21. Personal possession makes the Christian man; all else is mere talk. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps033.cfm

**v. 21**
- Barnes: "his holy name" means God himself, since the name often stands for the person. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/psalms/33.htm
- Henry: those who hope in God look forward to an eternal fulness of joy in his presence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_033.cfm

**v. 22**
- Clarke (Methodist): as we disclaim all merit, we seek for a continuance of thy mercy, and this we cannot expect but in a continual dependence on thee. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-33.html
- Guzik turns vv. 20–22 into a prayer for pastors after Sunday, a hope placed in God and not in one's gifts, effort or holiness. https://enduringword.com/the-preachers-heart-prays-psalm-33/
- Augustine links the verse to Romans 5:5: "hope confoundeth not." (ccel link above)
